Let’s reason through this.  

Soccer involves intermittent high-intensity activity (sprinting, jumping) and periods of lower intensity. Blood lactate concentration rises during intense bursts of exercise due to anaerobic glycolysis.  

- (A) “rarely increases above 3 mM” — This is false; in competitive soccer, blood lactate often exceeds 3 mM, sometimes reaching 6–10 mM after intense periods.  
- (B) “lower at the end of the game than at the end of the first half” — Unlikely; while lactate can accumulate in the first half, it tends to be even higher after the second half due to cumulative fatigue and possibly higher intensity toward the end.  
- (C) “higher at the end of the game than at the end of the first half” — This is plausible; studies show lactate levels often peak at the end of each half, but the highest levels are frequently seen after the second half.  
- (D) “increases throughout the course of the game” — Not accurate; lactate fluctuates with bursts of activity and recovery, not a continuous rise.  

The best-supported answer is that lactate is usually higher after the full game compared to halftime.  

Final answer: (C)
